chapters.title: Data, Information & File-Based Systems
chapters.description: Data processing, early computerisation, file-based systems, legacy systems and their limitations.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes data from information?

options.text: Data is raw material; information is data processed into a meaningful and usable form.
Data is always numerical; information is always textual.
Data is stored in files; information is stored only in databases.
Data is an output; information is an unprocessed input.

questions.explanation: The lectures define data as raw material and processing as the transformation that makes it meaningful and usable.
questions.source: Lectures 1–2 notes; Lecture 1 slides, slide 17; Lecture 2 slides, slide 2

questions.stem: In the input–process–output model, which item is the output of a payroll process?

options.text: Hours worked and hourly pay rates
Tax and deduction calculations
A completed payslip
The payroll application code

questions.explanation: Hours and rates are inputs, calculations are the process, and the payslip is the usable output.
questions.source: Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What was a major weakness of early business computerisation?

options.text: It redesigned every process before automating it.
It automated existing manual processes and preserved many of their inefficiencies.
It prevented departments from creating specialised applications.
It replaced all file storage with relational databases immediately.

questions.explanation: Early systems commonly copied manual workflows into software rather than redesigning how information was organised.
questions.source: Lectures 1–2 notes

questions.stem: Which description best matches a file-based system?

options.text: One central database serving every application through shared schemas
A collection of application programs in which each program defines and manages its own data
A spreadsheet containing several worksheets linked by formulas
A DBMS that exposes different external views to users

questions.explanation: In the file-based approach, individual programs provide services while separately defining and managing their own data.
questions.source: Lectures 1–2 notes; Connolly & Begg definition in lecture slides

questions.stem: A manager must manually combine printed HR, Sales and Accounts reports because the systems cannot exchange data. Which file-based limitation is most directly illustrated?

options.text: Separation and isolation of data
Controlled redundancy
Physical data independence
Query optimisation

questions.explanation: Departmental silos make cross-referenced searching and integrated reporting slow and difficult.
questions.source: Lecture 2 notes and slides, slides 12–13

questions.stem: A product has conflicting prices in two departmental files. Which data-quality problem is most direct?

options.text: Inconsistent copies undermine data integrity
The data is now physically independent of programs
The query has an alphabetical sort error
A mandatory relationship has become optional

questions.explanation: Different stored versions of the same fact cannot both supply a consistent current value.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–3, file-based limitations

questions.stem: What is program–data dependence?

options.text: Users must know SQL before accessing any stored data.
Application code is tightly tied to the physical structure or location of its data.
Programs can change without any effect on stored data.
One database program serves several unrelated organisations.

questions.explanation: In file-based systems, file structures and locations were hard-wired into application code, making changes expensive and risky.
questions.source: Lectures 1–3 notes

questions.stem: Why did fixed queries cause a proliferation of application programs?

options.text: Every new business question could require a newly coded program or report.
Fixed queries automatically copied every record into several files.
Each fixed query required a separate physical server.
Fixed queries prevented data from being stored permanently.

questions.explanation: A fixed query answers only a predetermined question, so new ad hoc information needs often required new code.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes and slides, slide 1

questions.stem: Why did two-digit year storage contribute to the Y2K problem?

options.text: Databases could not store numeric values larger than 99.
Systems could interpret “00” as 1900 rather than 2000.
Two-digit years always used more memory than four-digit years.
SQL standards prohibited four-digit dates before 2000.

questions.explanation: Developers saved scarce memory by storing two-digit years, but long-lived legacy systems could not reliably distinguish centuries.
questions.source: Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Which change best converts a fixed query into an ad hoc query capability?

options.text: Store the same report in several departments.
Allow users to vary search parameters without writing a new application.
Hard-code a single module code into the report.
Move the report file to a faster disk.

questions.explanation: Ad hoc querying lets users change the question or parameters while reusing the same query mechanism.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why should access to a student database depend on a user’s role?

options.text: Different roles need different data, and unnecessary access increases privacy and security risk
Every staff member should edit every record
Role-based access makes backups unnecessary
Sensitive data should be publicly searchable

questions.explanation: Least-necessary access protects sensitive information while allowing authorised work.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which is raw data rather than processed information?

options.text: A list of individual daily sales transactions
A report showing the best-selling product this month
A chart comparing monthly revenue trends
A warning that stock will run out tomorrow

questions.explanation: Raw observations become information after processing gives them context or meaning.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: For a supermarket stock system, which is an input?

options.text: A barcode scan recording a sale
A reordered-items report
A calculated stock balance
A management decision based on the report

questions.explanation: The scan supplies raw transaction data to the process.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: In a supermarket stock system, which activity transforms sales input into an updated stock value?

options.text: Print the final inventory report
Display a low-stock warning
Subtract sold quantities from the recorded stock level
Scan the product barcode

questions.explanation: The process transforms inputs; scanning is input and displaying or printing results is output.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2, input–process–output examples

questions.stem: Why did separate departmental files create data silos?

options.text: Each application controlled its own data and sharing across departments was difficult
Every department used one shared schema
All queries were ad hoc
Storage was centralised

questions.explanation: Application-owned files isolated related data in separate systems.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: A customer changes address, but only the Sales file is updated. What problem results?

options.text: Program–data independence improves
The query becomes ad hoc
The organisation now holds inconsistent copies of the same fact
The address becomes a calculated value

questions.explanation: Duplicate copies require multiple updates and can disagree when one is missed.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why does unnecessary duplication increase maintenance cost?

options.text: It guarantees perfect integrity
It reduces storage use
The same fact must be stored, checked and updated in several places
It eliminates all updates

questions.explanation: Multiple copies consume resources and create more opportunities for inconsistency.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does data integrity mean in this context?

options.text: The system contains no calculated fields
Data remain accurate, valid and consistent for their intended use
Every file uses the same font
All users have unrestricted access

questions.explanation: Integrity concerns the trustworthiness and consistency of stored values.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why does changing a file layout break a program in a program-dependent system?

options.text: The database automatically rewrites the application
The operating system deletes all data
Queries cannot contain fields
The program is written around the old physical structure and positions

questions.explanation: Tight coupling means the program must change when the data format changes.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What is file incompatibility?

options.text: A report uses a chart
Different applications store data in formats or structures that cannot be combined easily
Two users read the same database table
A field has a validation rule

questions.explanation: Incompatible encodings, layouts or definitions obstruct data sharing.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: A file application contains hard-coded reports. A manager asks a new question not covered by them. What development burden is likely?

options.text: The physical storage order answers the question
The application automatically infers the missing report
A programmer must build or change a report program
An index alone supplies the required new report logic

questions.explanation: Fixed-query systems require programming changes for new information requests.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–3, fixed queries

questions.stem: What makes a legacy system difficult to replace?

options.text: Replacement cannot involve data conversion
Important processes and data depend on old technology and assumptions
Legacy systems contain no data
Old systems are always fully documented

questions.explanation: Dependencies, undocumented rules and conversion risk can make migration costly and dangerous.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: A file stores 99 and 00 without a century. What ambiguity appears at the year boundary?

options.text: The century can always be inferred from the two digits alone
00 necessarily refers to a missing value
The date must be interpreted as the first day of each month
00 may be interpreted as 1900 rather than 2000

questions.explanation: Omitting the century saves space but loses information needed for reliable date interpretation.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2, two-digit years

questions.stem: What database feature most directly reduces departmental inconsistency?

options.text: Hard-coded queries
A shared controlled store used by multiple applications
A separate customer file for every department
More printed reports

questions.explanation: Central management allows authorised applications to use one consistent representation.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which request best illustrates an ad hoc query?

options.text: A file is copied to a backup disk
A manager asks today for customers who bought a new product combination not covered by a standard report
Payroll runs the same scheduled report every Friday
A program prints a fixed invoice layout

questions.explanation: An ad hoc query answers an unanticipated question without a new application program.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 1–2 and reviewed notes

chapters.title: Database Evolution & Models
chapters.description: The move to centralised databases, redundancy, historical development and major database models.

questions.stem: Which definition best describes a database in the course material?

options.text: A single spreadsheet used by one department
An organised collection of centralised data serving multiple applications while controlling redundancy
Any file that stores data after a program closes
A programming language for retrieving records

questions.explanation: The database concept centralises organised data so that several applications can use it while redundancy is controlled.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes and slides, slide 5

questions.stem: How does data duplication differ from data redundancy in the lecture terminology?

options.text: Duplication repeats whole data; redundancy stores a value that could be derived from other stored values.
Duplication affects only text; redundancy affects only numbers.
Duplication is intentional; redundancy is always accidental.
There is no difference between the two terms.

questions.explanation: Duplication means keeping repeated copies, while redundancy can mean storing a value that is calculable from existing data.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Which value is the clearest example of redundant data that should normally be calculated?

options.text: An employee identification number
An employee’s hours worked
An employee’s hourly rate
Total pay when hours worked and hourly rate are already stored

questions.explanation: Total pay can be calculated from hours multiplied by hourly rate, so separately storing it may be unnecessary redundancy.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why did the relational model gain wider adoption than earlier hierarchical and network proposals?

options.text: It removed the need for software products.
Commercial vendors built usable implementations of it.
It stored all information in one unstructured file.
It eliminated relationships between records.

questions.explanation: The relational model moved beyond research because software companies commercialised tools based on the framework.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Which database model organises data primarily into tables connected by keys?

options.text: Hierarchical model
Object-oriented model
Relational model
Physical model

questions.explanation: The relational model uses tables, rows and columns, with primary and foreign keys linking data.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly characterises an object-oriented database?

options.text: Data is stored as objects containing attributes and methods.
Data is restricted to flat text files.
Relationships are prohibited.
Only SQL tables can be stored.

questions.explanation: Object-oriented databases store objects directly and use object references to connect them.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes and slides, slides 3–4

questions.stem: What is the main idea of an object-relational database?

options.text: Replace all tables with a strict hierarchy.
Keep relational tables and SQL while adding object-style features.
Store only images and maps.
Remove data types from relational tables.

questions.explanation: Object-relational systems preserve relational foundations while supporting features such as complex or user-defined types.
questions.source: Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: A payroll system mainly stores structured text and numeric values in tables. Which model does the course material recommend as the usual fit?

options.text: Relational
Object-oriented
Hierarchical
Physical-only

questions.explanation: Relational databases are well suited to structured tables containing text and numbers.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: A system must manage highly complex spatial objects and visual map structures. Which model may be more suitable according to the lecture example?

options.text: File-based
Object-oriented
Relational without relationships
Fixed-query

questions.explanation: The lecture identifies visualisations and spatial data as cases where an object-oriented model may fit better.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: Why is Microsoft Excel not treated as a DBMS in the course material?

options.text: It cannot display rows and columns.
It does not provide the same enforced database structures, integrity controls and scalable management as a DBMS.
It cannot calculate formulas.
It cannot store any text values.

questions.explanation: Although a spreadsheet resembles a table, it does not enforce database data types and integrity rules in the same way and can fail at scale.
questions.source: Lectures 3 and 6 notes

questions.stem: Which data-management approach dominated many 1950s business systems?

options.text: Relational cloud databases
Object-relational spatial systems
Document databases with web APIs
Separate application files

questions.explanation: Early computerisation largely reproduced manual file processing for individual applications.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which models were major database research directions in the 1960s before relational systems became dominant?

options.text: Only object-oriented models
No structured models existed
Hierarchical and network models
Spreadsheet and word-processing models

questions.explanation: Hierarchical and network approaches preceded the relational model’s commercial adoption.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What was Codd’s key contribution to database development?

options.text: The Python programming language
The concept of a paper file
A relational model based on organising data into tables and relationships
The first spreadsheet macro

questions.explanation: Codd formalised the relational approach that later underpinned commercial systems.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why did relational databases suit much business data?

options.text: Structured facts could be represented in tables and queried with a common language
They store only images and methods
They prohibit relationships
They require every value to be unstructured

questions.explanation: Business records often have regular attributes and relationships well represented by tables.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: In an object-oriented database, what may be stored with an object’s attributes?

options.text: A separate spreadsheet formula
Methods describing its behaviour
Only printed reports
SQL permissions only

questions.explanation: Objects can combine state with operations and references to other objects.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why did object-relational databases emerge?

options.text: To remove tables from every database
To replace all data with program code
To prevent the use of SQL
To retain relational tables while supporting more complex object-like data features

questions.explanation: They extend the relational model rather than discarding its established strengths.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does it mean that a database supports multiple applications?

options.text: Only one user can open the database
Every application keeps an unrelated copy
The database contains executable apps only
Different authorised programs can use the same controlled data resource

questions.explanation: Shared data reduce isolation and support consistent organisational use.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: When is redundancy controlled rather than wasteful duplication?

options.text: When an extra copy is deliberate, documented and managed for a justified purpose
Whenever every department stores its own version
When no one knows which copy is current
When the copy cannot be updated

questions.explanation: Controlled redundancy is intentional and governed, for example for performance or resilience.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why should total pay usually be calculated rather than independently stored in several places?

options.text: Storage is free
Payroll has no inputs
It can be derived from underlying values and stored copies may become inconsistent
Calculated values cannot be displayed

questions.explanation: Deriving the value from authoritative components avoids conflicting copies.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why should stock-on-hand often be updated from transactions rather than typed into several files?

options.text: Manual duplication guarantees accuracy
Each department needs a different truth
Transactions cannot change stock
Transaction-based calculation helps maintain one consistent current value

questions.explanation: Using controlled updates reduces inconsistent balances.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What risk arises when Excel’s row limit is exceeded during an import?

options.text: Excel automatically becomes a DBMS
Every row is encrypted
The workbook gains relational integrity constraints
Rows may be omitted or data may be lost without creating a managed database

questions.explanation: A spreadsheet limit can truncate large data sets and does not provide database safeguards.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which workload is the strongest fit for a relational model?

options.text: A complex 3D simulation whose objects contain specialised behaviour
Unstructured video editing timelines only
A single temporary calculator result
Customers, orders and products with regular fields and clear relationships

questions.explanation: Structured business entities map naturally to rows, columns and keys.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which workload may benefit from object-oriented or object-relational features?

options.text: A simple employee salary table only
A list of four department names
One Boolean flag
Geographic objects with complex shapes and behaviours

questions.explanation: Complex spatial or multimedia objects may need richer types than plain scalar columns.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: How does a database differ from one application’s private file?

options.text: It cannot be queried
It belongs to no organisation
It is an organised shared resource managed for use by multiple authorised purposes
It must contain only one record

questions.explanation: A database separates organisational data from a single application’s private storage.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why does the relational model remain dominant despite newer models?

options.text: It is the only model that can store any bytes
Law requires every system to use it
It eliminates all design work
Its simple structure, mature tools and broad fit for structured data remain valuable

questions.explanation: Dominance reflects practical usefulness and ecosystem maturity, not universal superiority.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 3 and reviewed notes

chapters.title: Three-Level Architecture & Data Hierarchy
chapters.description: External, conceptual and internal schemas, mappings, data independence and implementation structure.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the ANSI-SPARC three-level database architecture?

options.text: To force every user to see the same data
To separate user views, logical design and physical storage to support data independence
To store three identical copies of every record
To replace the DBMS with application code

questions.explanation: Separating external, conceptual and internal levels reduces direct dependence between applications and physical storage.
questions.source: Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: Which level defines customised views for different users or applications?

options.text: External level
Conceptual level
Internal level
Physical device level

questions.explanation: The external level exposes role-relevant subsets of the database to different users and applications.
questions.source: Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: Which level defines the complete logical structure of organisational data and its relationships?

options.text: External level
Conceptual level
Internal level
Operating-system level

questions.explanation: The conceptual schema represents entities, attributes, relationships, constraints and legal values across the organisation.
questions.source: Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: Which task belongs primarily to the internal level?

options.text: Choosing which fields a payroll clerk may view
Defining all organisational entities and relationships
Choosing file access methods, indexes, encryption and storage allocation
Writing a manager’s monthly report

questions.explanation: The internal level concerns physical implementation and storage details.
questions.source: Lectures 3–4 notes

questions.stem: What is the role of mappings in the three-level architecture?

options.text: They translate requests and results between external, conceptual and internal levels.
They create duplicate copies of each external view.
They prevent all communication between levels.
They convert every database into a spreadsheet.

questions.explanation: External–conceptual and conceptual–internal mappings allow the separated layers to communicate.
questions.source: Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why is data independence described as being achieved only “to an extent”?

options.text: Every user must manage physical storage personally.
The layers remain connected through mappings, so complete separation is impossible.
Conceptual schemas are always identical to external views.
Databases cannot be moved between servers.

questions.explanation: The layers are separated, but mappings must still connect them for the system to operate.
questions.source: Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: A DBA moves database files to a new server without changing the user-facing application. Which benefit is illustrated?

options.text: Fixed querying
Physical data independence
Data duplication
Program–data dependence

questions.explanation: Changes to physical storage can often be isolated from external views and application logic.
questions.source: Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the data hierarchy from largest to smallest?

options.text: Database → File → Record → Field → Byte → Bit
File → Database → Field → Record → Bit → Byte
Database → Record → File → Byte → Field → Bit
Bit → Byte → Field → Record → File → Database

questions.explanation: The lecture hierarchy is Database, File, Record, Field, Byte, Bit.
questions.source: Lecture 4 notes and slides, slide 3

questions.stem: In the data hierarchy, what does a record normally represent?

options.text: One binary digit
One character encoded as bits
One complete instance or row, such as one student
The full collection of organisational data

questions.explanation: A record groups related fields for one entity instance, corresponding broadly to a relational row.
questions.source: Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why might a database designer set a reasonable character limit for a text field?

options.text: To prevent the DBMS from using indexes
To allocate storage more efficiently and constrain the permitted structure
To convert text automatically into integers
To create a new external schema

questions.explanation: Appropriate field sizes reduce wasted storage and form part of the implementation structure.
questions.source: Lecture 4 notes

questions.stem: Why might Payroll and a line manager receive different external views of employee data?

options.text: Each role should see only the fields and records needed for its work
The conceptual schema can contain only one employee
Internal storage changes for every user
External views remove all security needs

questions.explanation: Tailored views support usefulness and data minimisation.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: How can external views support GDPR-style data minimisation?

options.text: They prevent authorised access to all data
They change bytes into bits
They can hide personal data that a role does not need
They duplicate every field into public files

questions.explanation: Restricting exposure reduces unnecessary processing of personal information.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Where should the organisation-wide relationship between Customer and Order be defined?

options.text: In the disk sector map only
In a printed report
At the conceptual level
Only in one user’s external view

questions.explanation: The conceptual schema captures the complete logical structure and relationships.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which decision belongs most directly to the internal level?

options.text: Which fields a cashier may see
Whether Customer relates to Order
What a manager calls a report
How an index is stored to speed retrieval

questions.explanation: The internal level concerns physical storage and access structures.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: At which level is a column’s logical data type and validation meaning primarily defined?

options.text: No level represents types
Only in a user manual
Conceptual level, with implementation details supported internally
External level only

questions.explanation: Logical definitions belong to the organisation-wide schema, while physical representation is handled internally.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does an external–conceptual mapping do?

options.text: Copies disk sectors into a spreadsheet
Defines electrical network cables
Replaces every application
Connects a user view to the relevant parts of the logical schema

questions.explanation: Mappings translate between representations at adjacent levels.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does a conceptual–internal mapping do?

options.text: Creates a new business entity
Removes all indexes
Links logical structures to their physical storage representation
Assigns staff roles to reports

questions.explanation: It tells the DBMS how conceptual records and relationships are realised internally.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which architecture cardinality is expected in the three-level model?

options.text: Many external schemas, one conceptual schema and one internal schema
One external schema per field and no conceptual schema
Many conceptual schemas with no internal level
Exactly one schema at every level

questions.explanation: Multiple user views map to a single integrated logical design and physical implementation.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: A DBA changes an access method while preserving the logical schema. Which kind of independence is being used?

options.text: Program–data dependence on record position
Logical dependence of all user views
Physical data independence
A change in the enterprise’s business rules

questions.explanation: Physical independence separates storage implementation from the logical schema.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4, ANSI-SPARC architecture

questions.stem: A DBA changes a logical field in a way that also changes its meaning for applications. Why may programs still need updates?

options.text: External–conceptual mappings eliminate every logical dependency
Any storage change necessarily changes every user’s view
Data independence is limited when interfaces or meanings change
Adding layers means no mapping needs maintenance

questions.explanation: The layers are connected by mappings; independence is not a guarantee against changes in meaning or interface.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4, mappings and data independence

questions.stem: How many bits make one byte in the data hierarchy used in class?
questions.explanation: A byte consists of eight bits.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does a field represent in a record?

options.text: One attribute value, such as an employee’s surname
The entire database
A collection of files
One binary digit only

questions.explanation: Fields hold individual data items that together form a record.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why is an index described as an access structure?

options.text: It replaces the conceptual schema
It provides a faster route to records without scanning everything
It changes every value’s meaning
It grants every user administrator rights

questions.explanation: An index stores lookup information that can speed retrieval.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What is a pointer in low-level storage terms?

options.text: A stored reference to another location or record
A user-facing chart
A data-validation rule only
A complete database model

questions.explanation: Pointers help internal structures connect or locate stored data.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What DBA task is involved when moving a database to new infrastructure?

options.text: Deleting the conceptual schema
Planning migration, storage, access and continuity while preserving correct use
Changing every employee’s job title
Writing only external reports

questions.explanation: Database administration includes controlled migration and privilege management.
questions.source: IS2206 Lectures 3–4 and reviewed notes

chapters.title: DBMS Benefits, Components & Database Languages
chapters.description: Database trade-offs, DBMS processing, transaction handling, security and SQL language categories.

questions.stem: Which is a grounded advantage of centralised database storage?

options.text: Every user receives unrestricted access to all records.
Data integrity and consistency can be managed more uniformly.
The database can never fail.
No hardware or conversion costs are required.

questions.explanation: Central management makes it easier to apply integrity rules, security policies and consistent formats.
questions.source: Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: What is controlled redundancy?

options.text: Duplicating all records in every department
Allowing deliberate duplication only where it serves a justified need
Removing every backup copy from the system
Preventing any value from being calculated

questions.explanation: A DBMS aims to minimise unnecessary repetition while allowing managed redundancy where required.
questions.source: Lectures 3 and 5 notes

questions.stem: Which disadvantage follows from centralising critical operations in one database?

options.text: No user can access the data concurrently.
A failure can become a high-impact single point of failure.
The system cannot enforce one date format.
Ad hoc queries become impossible.

questions.explanation: If the central database goes down, many dependent operations may stop together.
questions.source: Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: What is the main function of a DBMS?

options.text: To organise data so it can be retrieved, modified and updated while mediating between applications and storage
To replace all users with automated scripts
To store only unstructured documents
To make every database application use an identical interface

questions.explanation: The DBMS manages database operations and separates logical access from physical data files.
questions.source: Lectures 4–5 notes

questions.stem: Which DBMS component checks whether a user has permission to perform a requested operation?

options.text: Buffer manager
Authorisation control
Integrity checker
Query output formatter

questions.explanation: Authorisation control verifies identity and privileges before allowing the request to continue.
questions.source: Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: A student’s date of birth is entered as a date that would make the student an infant. Which DBMS component should reject it?

options.text: Integrity checker
Recovery manager
Buffer manager
External schema mapper

questions.explanation: The integrity checker validates values against rules before they are accepted.
questions.source: Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: What is the transaction manager responsible for?

options.text: Designing every external user interface
Scheduling and coordinating concurrent operations, including conflicts
Writing all backup files manually
Defining the organisation’s mission statement

questions.explanation: The transaction manager coordinates simultaneous requests so conflicting work does not corrupt data.
questions.source: Lecture 5 notes

questions.stem: What is the recovery manager’s role?

options.text: To sort query results alphabetically
To keep transaction logs and support restoration to a consistent state after failure
To grant and revoke user privileges
To choose the entities in a conceptual model

questions.explanation: Recovery management records transaction activity so the database can be restored after corruption or failure.

Data Manipulation Language (DML)

Granting user privileges

DCL
HTML

DCL
DDL
DML

Conversion never affects users
Old files automatically map perfectly
Data, programs and working practices may all need cleansing, redesign and migration

SQL has no execution engine
Its security, concurrency and general services add overhead

The colour of external views
The number of database models
The size of printed reports

Backups replace integrity rules
A DBMS cannot fail
Recovery needs trustworthy copies and logs to restore data after serious failure

It removes the need for judgement
It can give authorised staff timely query access for lower-level decisions
It restricts all information to programmers

It removes the schema
Users can ask new questions without building a separate file-processing program for each one
It guarantees every query is correct

Buffer manager

External view designer only
Integrity checker
Buffer manager

chapters.title: Relational Model & Conceptual Modelling
chapters.description: Data-model components, conceptual design, entities, attributes, integrity and relational structures.

questions.stem: What is a data model?

options.text: A single diagram showing physical disk sectors
An integrated collection of concepts for describing data, relationships and constraints
A list of SQL keywords used by one vendor
A copy of every user’s external view

questions.explanation: A data model provides concepts for describing organisational data, how it relates and the rules that constrain it.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes; Lecture 6 slides, slide 1

questions.stem: Which three components may make up a data model?

options.text: Input, process and output
Structural part, manipulative part and integrity rules
Rows, reports and passwords
Files, programs and printers

questions.explanation: The lecture identifies structural, manipulative and integrity-rule components.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: What is the goal of conceptual modelling?

options.text: To define complete organisational data requirements independently of implementation details
To decide the exact disk sectors used by each record
To grant permissions to every employee
To write all application screens before identifying the data

questions.explanation: Conceptual modelling focuses on what data the organisation needs and how it relates, without choosing physical storage or a DBMS.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: In a relational table, what is an attribute?

options.text: A column describing a characteristic of an entity
A complete row representing one instance
A relationship between two databases
A transaction log entry

questions.explanation: Attributes become table columns and describe entity characteristics.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: In a relational table, what does a row represent?

options.text: A data type shared by a column
One individual record or entity instance
A physical storage device
A set of user privileges

questions.explanation: Each row is a record for one instance, such as one student or staff member.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: What does it mean for a value to be atomic?

options.text: It must be encrypted.
It must be a single, indivisible value rather than a list or sub-structure.
It must be a number.
It must appear in several tables.

questions.explanation: Atomicity at the cell level means storing one value per cell.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: Why should all entries in one column normally share a data type?

options.text: To support consistent validation and operations on that attribute
To make every table contain only one row
To eliminate the need for a column name
To turn the table into an external schema

questions.explanation: A column represents one attribute, so a consistent type lets the DBMS enforce valid values and operations.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: Why is storing a person’s current age often a poor design choice?

options.text: Age can never be represented numerically.
Age changes over time and would need repeated updates.
Age cannot be used in a query.
Age always violates user permissions.

questions.explanation: A date of birth is stable, whereas a stored age becomes outdated and introduces maintenance problems.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: What creates the “third dimension” described in the relational model lecture?

options.text: Adding colour to a table
Relationships between rows in different tables through shared values
Storing three copies of every column
Using three data types in one cell

questions.explanation: Rows and columns form a two-dimensional table; links between tables add the relational dimension.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes

questions.stem: Which item is most likely to be modelled as an entity in a corner-shop database?

options.text: Product
Expensive
Quickly
Calculate

questions.explanation: Entities are persistent people, places, objects or events worth storing; Product fits that definition.
questions.source: Lecture 6 notes and slides, slide 10

questions.stem: Which is an object-based data model category?

options.text: A model representing entities, attributes and relationships at a high conceptual level
A disk-sector layout only
A printed file listing
A byte encoding standard

questions.explanation: Object-based conceptual models describe real-world things and their associations.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which is a record-based data model?

options.text: A network cable plan
The relational model
A CPU cache map
A paper form colour scheme

questions.explanation: Record-based models organise data as fixed-format records; relational tables are the main course example.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does a physical data model describe?

options.text: How data are organised and accessed in storage
Only users’ business vocabulary
A list of stakeholder opinions
The visual style of a form

questions.explanation: Physical models focus on implementation-level structures.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why should conceptual modelling be independent of a chosen DBMS?

options.text: Requirements should be understood before adapting them to product-specific storage features
A DBMS contains no schema
Implementation never affects design
Conceptual models cannot show relationships

questions.explanation: Separating requirements from technology avoids forcing the problem into a premature solution.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Which characteristic makes Customer a strong entity candidate?

options.text: It is a persistent thing about which the organisation stores facts
It is a one-time calculation result
It is a formatting preference
It is one letter in a name

questions.explanation: Entities represent identifiable things of continuing organisational interest.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: In a Customer entity, what is Email Address?

options.text: A query language
An attribute describing the customer
A separate database level
A DBMS component

questions.explanation: Attributes record properties of an entity.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: Why should a full name and a current age not be stored together as one relational field?

options.text: A single field must always use a numeric data type
They combine facts that may need separate validation and querying
They are necessarily foreign-key values
Every descriptive attribute must form part of the primary key

questions.explanation: Atomic design separates meaningful values; age also changes over time.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6, relational attributes and atomic values

questions.stem: Why might First Name and Surname be stored separately?

options.text: A person can have only one name part
They can be searched, sorted and validated independently
Separate fields remove all duplicate names
SQL cannot concatenate text

questions.explanation: Splitting meaningful components supports flexible use while each field remains atomic.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: A customer database stores date of birth and needs a current age report. Why derive age instead of maintaining a separate current-age field?

options.text: Age changes with time while date of birth is stable
Dates cannot be stored in relational tables
A derived report cannot be queried
Age must always be a primary key

questions.explanation: A stored current age can become stale without updates.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6, date of birth versus age

questions.stem: How is a relationship between Order and Customer commonly represented in a relational design?

options.text: The rows must be physically adjacent
The relationship exists only in a report title
A shared key value links each order to its customer
Both tables use different unrelated values

questions.explanation: Matching key values connect records across tables.

questions.stem: What does the structure component of a data model define?

options.text: Only backup frequency
How data items and relationships are organised
Which users like the system
The current market price

questions.explanation: Structure specifies the elements and associations represented by the model.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does the manipulation component of a data model define?

options.text: The number of users only
Operations for retrieving and changing data
The office floor plan
The colour of tables

questions.explanation: A usable model includes ways to query and update its structures.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What does the integrity component of a data model define?

options.text: Only data-entry speed
A marketing plan
Rules that keep stored states valid and consistent
A list of printer settings

questions.explanation: Constraints restrict data to acceptable values and relationships.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: In a corner-shop model, which is most likely an attribute rather than an entity?

options.text: Supplier
Product
Customer
Product price

questions.explanation: Price describes a product, while suppliers, products and customers are persistent things.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture 6 and reviewed notes

questions.stem: What should follow a completed conceptual model?

options.text: Give every user internal storage access
Combine all facts into one field
Translate it into a suitable logical and physical design for the chosen technology
Discard the requirements

questions.stem: In a basic SQL query, what does the SELECT clause specify?

The columns or expressions to return
The user privileges to grant
The physical file location

questions.stem: What does the asterisk mean in SELECT * FROM emp?

options.text: Return all columns from EMP
Multiply all numeric values in EMP
Return only unique rows
Sort EMP in descending order

questions.explanation: In this query, * requests every column from the source table.
questions.source: Tutorial 1; SQL Lab 1, p. 9; SQL Lab 2, p. 2

questions.stem: What is the purpose of DISTINCT in SELECT DISTINCT job FROM emp?

options.text: Sort job values alphabetically
Remove duplicate job values from the result
Change all job values to uppercase
Delete duplicate rows from the stored table

questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the displayed result without changing stored data.
questions.source: Tutorial 1; SQL Lab 2, p. 3

questions.stem: How does DISTINCT behave when several columns are selected?

options.text: It checks uniqueness of the complete combination of selected values.
It checks only the first selected column.
It removes columns containing null values.
It sorts each selected column independently.

questions.explanation: With multiple columns, two result rows are duplicates only when the whole selected combination matches.

questions.stem: Which clause controls the sequence of rows in a query result?

options.text: FROM
DISTINCT
ORDER BY
LENGTH

Sorts departments low-to-high and names reverse-alphabetically
Removes repeated department and employee values
Joins department numbers to employee names

options.text: Tests whether two values are equal
Concatenates values and literal text in the output
Divides one numeric value by another
Removes duplicates from a result

options.text: To allow spaces and preserve the alias’s capitalisation
To convert the result into a number
To treat the alias as stored data
To make the alias a table name automatically

SUBSTR
LENGTH
RPAD

The last four characters of ENAME
ENAME padded to four characters
The number of characters in ENAME

Slide Sorter
Package Manager
Route Inspector

Object Storage
User Profile
Template Gallery

The table that supplies the rows
The columns to display
The sort direction

Rows sorted by salary automatically
The ename and sal columns for the displayed EMP rows
Every column except ename and sal

Ascending
Descending
Random

Salary descending only
Department descending and salary ascending

A filter condition
A table alias
Fixed text between the two values in the displayed result

comm * 12
sal + comm
All operations occur left to right regardless of precedence

They turn numbers into rows
They apply DISTINCT
They force the enclosed calculation to be evaluated first

questions.stem: What happens to an unquoted column alias in Oracle output?

options.text: It preserves every typed lowercase letter
It becomes a string literal
It sorts the rows
Oracle normally displays it in uppercase

questions.stem: What does UPPER(ename) return?

Only the first character
The employee name converted to uppercase
The original value permanently rewritten

questions.stem: What does LOWER(job) return?

The job text converted to lowercase
The shortest job title
The job’s character count

The record depends on related parent entities for its existence
The record can be drawn between two other boxes
The record uses a short name

Attribute length
Column order

Alphabetical sorting

Exactly one
Zero to many
One to many

A crow’s foot alone
A key label
A bar

One or many
Zero or many
Zero or one

All foreign keys

An enterprise-specific general constraint

A date seven days later

Choose the physical file location

Sort rows alphabetically automatically

All salaries outside the range

Both boundary values and the values between them

comm = NULL
comm = 'NULL'
comm = 0

Only if salary is also zero
No, zero and NULL are identical

A percentage calculation
Only one numeric digit

A missing database value

Exactly one character

Every name containing lowercase a

Names starting with uppercase A

Both conditions

To reduce unnecessary redundancy and improve the structure of relations
To choose the physical indexes for every query

An information model that does not commit to physical storage details

Only the job_title
A separate group for every input row even if both values match

chapters.title: Normalisation — Dependencies, 1NF, 2NF & 3NF

questions.stem: What does the functional dependency StudentID → StudentName mean?

options.text: Each StudentID determines exactly one StudentName within the relation.
Every StudentName uniquely identifies one StudentID.
StudentID and StudentName must have the same data type.
A student must have a different name in every row.

questions.explanation: A functional dependency runs from a determinant to a determined value. It does not automatically hold in the reverse direction.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture #12, 15 October 2026 — lecture notes and underlying transcript

questions.stem: A relation contains StudentID and LastName. Two students can share a last name, but each StudentID identifies one student. Which dependency follows from these rules?

options.text: LastName → StudentID, but StudentID cannot determine LastName.
Both directions must hold because both columns describe students.
Neither direction can hold unless the names are unique.
StudentID → LastName, but LastName need not determine StudentID.

questions.explanation: An identifier can determine a last name even when several identifiers share that same last name.
questions.source: IS2206 Lecture #12, 15 October 2026 — lecture notes and underlying transcript

questions.stem: A Student table stores "EC2204, IS2206" as two separate module codes in a single Modules cell. Which normalisation requirement is directly violated?

options.text: Second normal form: dependence on the whole composite key.

First normal form: one value per row–column intersection.

questions.explanation: The cell contains a list of separate module values rather than one atomic value in the intended representation.

The columns represent a repeating group rather than separate enrolment rows.
The table necessarily has no possible candidate key.
All repeated StudentID values in any related table must be deleted.

questions.explanation: Numbered columns for the same kind of fact encode a repeating group. Enrolment facts should be represented in a structure that supports separate rows.

questions.stem: A spreadsheet shows a student’s ID only beside their first module, leaving ID blank beside their other module rows. Why fill in the corresponding ID when flattening this data?

options.text: So each module row explicitly identifies the student to whom it belongs.
So StudentID becomes unique in the combined enrolment table.
So all students are assigned the same module result.
So module rows can be counted without preserving student identity.

questions.explanation: A query filtering by student ID cannot associate blank-ID rows with that student merely because a person can infer the association visually.

questions.stem: When repeating enrolment data is moved out of a Student relation, why retain StudentID in the enrolment relation?

options.text: It makes every enrolment a different student.
It prevents a student from taking more than one module.
It replaces the need to identify which module was taken.
It preserves the link between each enrolment and the student.

questions.explanation: Copying the original key into the separated relation maintains the relationship between the two sets of facts.

questions.stem: Enrolment(StudentID, ModuleCode, Credits, Result) has sole candidate key (StudentID, ModuleCode). Students take each module at most once; Credits depends only on ModuleCode. What kind of dependency is ModuleCode → Credits?

options.text: A full dependency on both parts of the candidate key.
A repeating group that necessarily violates atomicity.
A partial dependency of a non-key attribute on part of the composite key.
A dependency that makes ModuleCode alone a key for Enrolment.

questions.stem: In a simple enrolment model, each student takes a module at most once, and different students may get different results in different modules. Why does Result depend on (StudentID, ModuleCode) as a whole?

options.text: The module code alone determines every student’s result.
Both the student and the module are needed to identify the relevant result.
The student ID alone determines the same result for all their modules.
A numerical result cannot be functionally dependent on a key.

questions.explanation: The result belongs to a particular student–module combination, not to the student or module in isolation.

questions.stem: Enrolment(StudentID, ModuleCode, Credits, Result) has sole candidate key (StudentID, ModuleCode). Credits depends only on ModuleCode; Result needs the whole key. Which decomposition removes the partial dependency while retaining the results?

options.text: Module(ModuleCode, Credits) and Enrolment(StudentID, ModuleCode, Result).
Student(StudentID, Credits) and Module(ModuleCode, Result).
Module(ModuleCode, Credits, Result) and Student(StudentID).
Enrolment(StudentID, Credits, Result), with ModuleCode discarded.

questions.explanation: Module-level credits are stored once per module. Student-specific results remain with the student–module combination.

questions.stem: A module’s credit value is copied into every student’s enrolment row. Some rows are changed when the credit value changes, but others are not. What problem has occurred?

options.text: A successful lossless decomposition.
A failure of atomicity merely because the value is numeric.
A proof that Result depends only on ModuleCode.
An update anomaly caused by storing the same fact repeatedly.

questions.explanation: Multiple copies of a module-level fact can become inconsistent when an update does not reach every copy.

questions.stem: A table stores module details only alongside enrolments. You cannot record a new module until someone enrols. Which problem does this illustrate?

options.text: A deletion anomaly: removing a row destroys unrelated existing facts.
A partial dependency that has already been removed.
An insertion anomaly: one fact cannot be recorded independently of another.
A lossless join: smaller relations reconstruct the original.

questions.explanation: Recording the module is unnecessarily tied to having an enrolment row. Separating module facts can remove that dependency between insertions.

questions.stem: A combined module–enrolment table contains the only copy of a module’s details. Deleting its last enrolment also removes those details. What is this called?

options.text: An insertion anomaly.
A deletion anomaly.
Dependency preservation.
Full functional dependency.

questions.explanation: Deleting one kind of fact, an enrolment, has unintentionally removed another fact, the module’s details.

questions.stem: A relation is in 1NF and all its candidate keys consist of a single attribute. What follows about partial dependencies on those keys?

options.text: There is no proper part of a composite candidate key on which a non-key attribute could depend.
Every non-key attribute must therefore be independent of every key.
Transitive dependencies are impossible as well.
The relation must still contain a repeating group.

questions.explanation: Single-attribute candidate keys cannot have the partial-key dependency targeted by 2NF. This does not remove the need to check for 3NF problems.

questions.stem: Student(StudentID, StudentName, DepartmentID, DepartmentName) has sole candidate key StudentID. Each student has one department; DepartmentID determines DepartmentName. What is the relevant dependency chain?

options.text: DepartmentName → StudentID → DepartmentID.
StudentName → DepartmentName → StudentID.
DepartmentID → StudentID → StudentName.
StudentID → DepartmentID → DepartmentName.

questions.explanation: The department name is determined through the department identifier rather than being a fact specific to the student.

questions.stem: Student(StudentID, StudentName, DepartmentID, DepartmentName) has sole candidate key StudentID, and DepartmentID → DepartmentName. Which split addresses the transitive dependency while keeping each student’s department?

options.text: Student(StudentID, StudentName) and Department(DepartmentID, DepartmentName), with no student–department link.
Student(StudentID, DepartmentName) and Department(DepartmentID, StudentName).
Student(StudentID, StudentName, DepartmentID) and Department(DepartmentID, DepartmentName).
Student(StudentID, StudentName, DepartmentName), with DepartmentID deleted.

questions.explanation: DepartmentName belongs with its determinant DepartmentID. Keeping DepartmentID in Student preserves the association.

questions.stem: A relation is in 2NF and has a single-attribute primary key. Why should it still be checked for 3NF?

options.text: A single-attribute primary key necessarily contains a partial dependency.
A non-key attribute may determine another non-key attribute, creating a transitive dependency.
2NF allows lists in cells, so atomicity must first be introduced.
3NF requires replacing every single-attribute key with a composite key.

questions.explanation: Removing partial dependencies does not establish that non-key facts are free from transitive dependencies.

questions.stem: Which progression correctly matches the introductory normalisation checks?

options.text: 1NF: remove repeating groups; 2NF: remove partial dependencies; 3NF: remove transitive dependencies.
1NF: remove transitive dependencies; 2NF: remove repeating groups; 3NF: remove partial dependencies.
1NF: remove partial dependencies; 2NF: remove transitive dependencies; 3NF: remove repeating groups.
1NF: remove foreign keys; 2NF: remove primary keys; 3NF: remove candidate keys.

questions.explanation: Each stage builds on the previous one: atomic representation comes before the partial- and transitive-dependency checks.

questions.stem: A table has atomic cells, but its sole candidate key is (StudentID, ModuleCode) and it stores StudentName, which depends only on StudentID. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: Atomic cells alone establish 3NF.
The composite key means it must fail 1NF.
The partial dependency means no functional dependencies exist.
It can satisfy 1NF while failing 2NF.

questions.explanation: Atomicity and full-key dependence are different requirements. Meeting the first does not establish the second.

questions.stem: What does a lossless decomposition allow you to do?

options.text: Keep only the rows that occur most frequently in the original relation.
Remove the original key and infer missing links from row order.
Reconstruct the original relation exactly by joining the resulting smaller relations.
Ignore the original dependencies as long as column names are retained.

questions.explanation: Losslessness concerns preserving the original information so that decomposition does not change the facts reconstructed by joining.

questions.stem: What is dependency preservation intended to achieve when a relation is decomposed?

options.text: Every original column must appear in every resulting relation.
The original dependency constraints can be enforced through constraints on the smaller relations.
All resulting relations must use exactly the same primary key.
The original relation must remain as an additional duplicate table.

questions.explanation: Decomposition must preserve the data’s rules as well as its information. Dependency preservation is distinct from lossless reconstruction.

questions.stem: Normalisation aims to minimise redundant facts. Why can a DepartmentID still appear in many Student rows?

options.text: It acts as a foreign key linking multiple students to a department.
Foreign-key values are exempt from all integrity constraints.
Each repeated DepartmentID represents a new department with the same identifier.
A repeated foreign key proves every student has the same primary key.

questions.explanation: Repeated linking identifiers maintain relationships; this differs from unnecessarily copying all the department’s descriptive details into every student row.

questions.stem: Why must attribute meanings and business rules be understood before deciding functional dependencies?

options.text: Dependencies are determined solely by alphabetical column order.
Every column with a numeric data type is a determinant.
Any two columns with different names are necessarily independent.
Dependencies express constraints on valid data, not just coincidences in the current sample.

questions.explanation: A small sample can suggest a pattern without establishing that it must hold for all valid records. The lecturer explicitly warned against guessing relationships.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the first three normal forms?

options.text: 3NF replaces atomicity, so repeating groups become acceptable again.
A relation must choose either 1NF, 2NF or 3NF, never more than one.
A relation in 3NF also satisfies the requirements of 1NF and 2NF.
2NF is checked before any 1NF requirements are considered.

questions.explanation: The normal forms form a progression; later stages retain the requirements of earlier stages.

questions.stem: A heavily decomposed database needs many joins for a frequently used report and has demonstrated poor performance. What trade-off motivates considering controlled denormalisation?

options.text: Adding redundancy automatically improves integrity without further controls.
Potentially faster access must be balanced against extra redundancy and the need to maintain consistency.
Any slow query proves normalisation was conceptually invalid.
Merging tables removes the need to enforce business rules.

questions.explanation: The lecture discusses balancing integrity against application performance. Denormalisation can reintroduce duplicated facts, so it is not a reason to abandon consistency controls.

questions.stem: A table has sole candidate key (StudentID, ModuleCode). StudentName depends only on StudentID; Result depends on both key attributes. Which change addresses the partial dependency without losing the association?

options.text: Store StudentName in Student(StudentID, StudentName) and retain StudentID, ModuleCode and Result in Enrolment.
Move Result into Student and remove ModuleCode from the database.
Keep StudentName in Enrolment and delete StudentID from every row.
Store one Result per ModuleCode, shared by all students.

questions.explanation: StudentName describes the student, whereas Result describes the enrolment. Separating the student fact removes its partial dependency in the combined table.
